text: The most trusted defense against adversarial examples is called adversarial training, and it comes from folding the attack directly into the training process itself. Instead of hoping a model generalizes to perturbed inputs it never saw, you generate those perturbed inputs on purpose, during training, and make the model learn to classify them correctly too. That idea, formalized by Madry and colleagues in 2018, is still the baseline every later robustness claim gets measured against.

Here's the real cost, documented in the research, not theoretical. Tsipras and colleagues showed in 2019 that adversarially robust models frequently score lower on ordinary, unperturbed inputs than a standard model trained the normal way. Add to that a real compute cost: generating adversarial examples at every training step can multiply total training time several times over. Robust accuracy goes up. Clean accuracy and training budget both take a hit.

The attack used to generate those training examples is usually Projected Gradient Descent, or PGD — a stronger, iterative cousin of the single-step method from lesson seventeen. Each training step crafts a fresh adversarial version of the batch, computes the model's loss against it, and updates the weights to do better next time. That extra loop, repeated across the whole training run, is exactly where the added compute cost comes from.

Not every defense survives contact with a better attack. Defensive distillation looked like a cheap win in 2016, until Carlini and Wagner showed it mainly broke the gradient-based attacks used to test it, without closing the real vulnerability — a differently designed attack went straight through. Athalye and colleagues later found the same pattern across a whole set of proposed defenses and named it obfuscated gradients: robustness that evaporates the moment you test with an attack built knowing the defense is there.

Randomized smoothing takes a different approach entirely: instead of surviving known attacks, it provides a mathematical guarantee that a prediction can't change within a bounded perturbation radius, by averaging over many noisy copies of the same input. That guarantee is real and provable — but it costs extra compute at inference time, and it only covers perturbations inside that certified radius.

No technique here removes the risk; each one trades accuracy, compute, or scope for a measurable amount of protection. The real question for a security team isn't which defense to trust — it's how you'd actually go about testing one before you trust it. That's next.
